why.correct: The legend title and the classes (millions, a billion) show a total: the number of people in each country.
options: Right: the legend title is "Total population (number of people)", and the classes are counts of people.
That would be people per unit of land, a rate. The legend counts people and says nothing about land area.
Growth needs numbers from two dates. This map shows one count, from 2024.
A share is a percent. The classes here are counts in millions and billions, not percents.

why.correct: A good pattern statement names the places and the values: India at 1 billion or more, Bhutan under 10 million.
options: Read the shades again: India is the darkest; Bangladesh is one class lower, with Pakistan.
Right: it names places, their classes and the values of those classes.
The map has four classes in use, from Bhutan (lightest) to India (darkest).
Sri Lanka is in the 10 to 99 million class and Pakistan in the 100 to 999 million class; Bhutan is the lightest.

why.correct: Totals on a shaded map favor big countries. To judge crowding you need people per unit of land, which this map does not show.
options: The map does have a source line: UN World Population Prospects 2024.
The legend runs from light (under 10 million) to dark (1 billion or more), so dark means high.
Right: a total says nothing about how much land the people share. Bangladesh is small and very crowded (UN WPP 2024), yet it is a class lighter than India.
India is marked on the map and shaded in the darkest class.

why.correct: River Town's line rises from 20 to 50 (thousands of people): a rising trend over 30 years.
options: Read the years along the bottom: 1990 is on the left, so the line rises over time.
That is close to Hill Town's 1990 value, not River Town's line.
River Town's line rises in each decade; it is Hill Town that falls after 1990.
Right: a trend gives the direction, the dates and the size of the change.

why.correct: The lines cross near 2000, where both towns had about 28,000 people.
options: Right: both lines are at about 28 (thousand) in 2000.
In 1990 Hill Town had about 30,000 people and River Town about 20,000.
By 2010 River Town (about 38,000) had passed Hill Town (about 25,000).
In 2020 the gap was widest: about 50,000 against about 22,000.

why.correct: A chart shows what changed and when. Why it changed is a claim that needs more evidence.
options: The chart never shows people moving between the towns; one town may have grown for other reasons.
Right: the chart shows how many people, not why. A reason needs another source, such as interviews or job data.
Jobs are not on the chart at all, while the number of people is.
Hill Town shrank, and the units (thousands of people) are on the axis.

why.correct: A useful source line names who made the data and when. Without a year you cannot tell how out of date a number is.
options: It names no maker and no year, so you cannot check it or know how old it is.
A website is not a named source, and there is no year.
Right: it names who made the data and the year of the data.
"Recent" is not a year. Numbers like these change, so a year matters.

why.correct: Share = part / whole x 100 = <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{10{,}000}{40{,}000} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 25\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
Read the unit in the header. "Per 1,000 people" is a rate, so it compares how well each town is served, not how many beds each has.
options: A rate does not give a total. If Town Q has many more people, it could have as many beds or more.
The table gives no populations, so you cannot tell which town is bigger.
The 2 is a rate, 2 beds for each 1,000 people, not a count of beds.
Right: the unit is a rate, beds for each 1,000 people, and 4 is more than 2.

why.correct: Start with what the figure is about, learn what its marks and units mean, check where the data came from, and only then describe the pattern.
Ask what unit each number describes. Each shade is one province, so the scale of analysis is local (subnational), not national.
options: Right: the scale of analysis is set by the unit each value describes. Here that unit is a province, a part of the country.
This is the common slip. The map covers one country, but each shade describes one province, so the data are subnational.
Global data would have values for countries across the world. This map has values for provinces in one country.
The regional scale is a group of countries. Each value here is for one province inside one country.

why.correct: One national number can hide large differences between provinces. Reading the data at a smaller scale shows them.
options: The shades run from under 40% to 80% or more, so the provinces are far from equal.
Right: a national average blends high and low provinces into one number. The map shows the gap.
The map counts no homes and shows no other country.
A rise needs data from two dates. This map shows one date.

why.correct: Match the scale of the data to the scale of the decision: a choice between provinces needs data by province.
options: The national figure gives one number for the whole country, so it cannot rank the provinces.
A world map would show Country A as a single value and hide its provinces.
Right: the choice is between provinces, so the data must be for provinces.
The province data are the right scale, but the highest access is where new lines are needed least.

why.correct: The scale of analysis is the unit of the data (here, countries), not the size of the area the map covers.
options: The map's size is the world, but the unit each value describes is a country.
The measure is about cities, but each value is a share for a whole country.
No values are given for groups of countries; each country has its own.
Right: each value describes one country, even though the map covers the world.

why.correct: <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 \times 50{,}000 = 200{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> cm on the ground, and <math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{200{,}000}{100{,}000}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="hug-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2</annotation></semantics></math> km, because 100,000 cm make 1 km.
In map scale, "large scale" means the fraction 1:denominator is large, so features look large and the area shown is small. It is the opposite of what the words suggest.
options: Right: 1:5,000 is the biggest fraction, so things look large and the map shows a small area in detail.
This is the smallest fraction, so it is the smallest-scale map: a large area with little detail.
A continent at 1:20,000,000 is a small-scale map: things look tiny.
A whole country at 1:10,000,000 is a small-scale map, even though the country is large.

why.correct: Global covers the world, regional a group of countries (such as South Asia), national one country, and local a part of a country (a province, city or neighborhood).
Map scale is a ratio. A large-scale map has a large fraction (like 1:5,000), so it shows a small area in detail.
options: Map scale is about the fraction, not a middle size. A country map is usually small scale.
Right: large scale means a large fraction (1:5,000), so the area is small and the detail is high.
This repeats the student's mistake: a small-scale map covers more ground.
Map scale and scale of analysis are different ideas; a large-scale map can show local data.

why.correct: Name the scale from the unit of the data (provinces), then name the places at each end of the pattern.
A single national number blends very different places. Looking at the local scale shows the real pattern: crowded along the Nile, nearly empty in the desert.
options: National data are useful for comparing countries; they hide differences inside a country.
The question says the opposite: people live in the valley and delta, not across the desert.
Right: averaging the crowded valley with the nearly empty desert gives a moderate number that describes neither.
Neither scale is more accurate; each answers a different question.

why.correct: An explain answer needs a cause, a link word (because, so) and an effect tied to the place asked about.
options: Right: "explain" asks for the how or why. "Jobs" names a factor; the link to moving is missing.
A correct name earns an identify point. An explain needs the link: why jobs make people move.
This part has no stimulus and asks for no number; it asks for a reason with its link.
Readers score what the verb demands, not the length. Here the verb demands a link that is missing.

why.correct: A full explain answer has every link: more paid jobs in the capital, so people move there to earn higher wages.
options: This says jobs matter but never says how they cause people to move.
Right: it gives the cause (more paid jobs), the link (so) and the effect (people move to earn more).
This lists more factors but links none of them to moving.
This restates the question and adds a description; restating earns nothing.

why.correct: Identify is the only verb a single word can satisfy. Every other verb asks for more.
options: Explain asks for the how or why, which a single word does not give.
Describe asks for features: what it is like, where and how much.
Right: identify asks you to name the thing; a word or phrase is enough.
Compare asks about two things and needs both sides.

why.correct: For "explain the degree", open with the degree (high, moderate or low), then give the reasoning.
options: Naming more places can help, but the missing piece is the degree the verb asks for.
The part does not ask for a definition.
No other country is part of the question.
Right: "explain the degree" asks you to state a degree first, then explain it. The explanation here is good; the degree is missing.

why.correct: Data for parts of a country are at the local (subnational) scale, even when the map shows the whole country.
options: Right: each value is for a province, a part of the country.
National data would give one value for the whole of Country A.
The regional scale is a group of countries.
The global scale compares places across the world.

why.correct: State the degree, then the because or so: "To a high degree: ... so ...".
options: A definition of province data does not state a degree or explain it.
Right: it states the degree first and keeps the reasoning with its "so".
Defining a clinic answers a different verb, define, about a different term.
This starts a comparison without stating a degree.

why.correct: Compare needs both sides: "A is ..., whereas B is ...".
options: Describe gives the features of one thing or pattern.
Identify names one thing.
Right: a compare answer says how two things are alike or different, and speaks of both.
Define gives the meaning of one term.

why.correct: A describe answer for a pattern says where, what and how much, with named places.
options: This names no place, so it does not describe a pattern a reader can check.
This gives a reason (an explain) instead of the pattern (a describe), and names no place.
This says farms exist but gives no where, what or how much, so it does not describe a pattern.
Right: it says where (along the river, in the south), what (most farms) and the contrast with the north.

why.correct: Place, cause, link word, effect: each link of the chain is written out.
Seven one-point parts, each checked against one rubric line: do exactly what each verb asks.
options: Right: seven parts, one point each, so each question is worth 7 points.
Writing more does not earn more points; each part has one point.
Readers score part by part, so a strong Part A cannot make up for a missing Part B.
Terms help only when they do what the verb asks; listing terms earns nothing.
